questions.question: Define the five population indicators covered in the lesson, and explain the age-structure trap that makes crude death rates misleading.
questions.expected_answer: The crude birth rate is the number of live births per thousand people per year (South Africa about 19; Mali above 40; South Korea below 6), with 'crude' meaning it is calculated across the whole population without adjusting for age. The crude death rate is deaths per thousand per year (South Africa about 9). The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would bear in her lifetime under current patterns, with replacement level at 2,1 — two children replacing two parents plus a margin for those who die young; South Africa has fallen from about six in the 1960s to about 2,3. The infant mortality rate is babies per thousand live births dying before their first birthday (Central African Republic above 70; Iceland and Finland below 2; South Africa about 25), treated as the most revealing measure of development because infant survival requires safe water, nutrition, vaccines, clinics and educated mothers all working at once. Life expectancy is the years a newborn can expect to live (Switzerland above 84; South Africa about 65, having fallen to about 53 during the Aids epidemic before the antiretroviral programme restored more than a decade). The death-rate trap: wealthy countries can post higher crude death rates than poor ones — Italy above 10 against Uganda below 6 — because age structure, not healthcare quality, drives the figure: Italy's large elderly population dies at higher rates in even the best care, while Uganda's population is overwhelmingly young. A low crude death rate may prove only youth, so always ask who makes up the population, and never judge a country from one indicator alone.

questions.question: Describe how a population pyramid is constructed, the three reading habits used to interpret one, and how the dependency ratio is calculated, including a worked example.
questions.expected_answer: A vertical axis runs up the centre; at each level a pair of horizontal bars extends back to back, males to the left and females to the right. Each level is a five-year age cohort, stacked from nought-to-four at the base upward to the oldest at the peak, and bar length shows the number or percentage of people of that age and sex. The three reading habits: first, inspect the base — a broad base means a high recent birth rate, while a base narrower than the bars above signals declining births; second, follow the slope of the sides — a sharp taper between cohorts means high mortality, while near-vertical sides mean most people survive to old age; third, hunt for irregularities — a notch (one cohort abruptly short) records a war, epidemic or famine that killed that generation or suppressed its births, a bulge records a baby boom or immigration at that age, and longer female bars at the top reflect women outliving men. The dependency ratio divides the population into young dependants (0-14), the economically active (15-64) and aged dependants (65+), then computes (young + aged) divided by economically active, times 100, giving dependants per hundred workers. Worked example: with 30% under fifteen and 6% over sixty-four, dependants are 36% against 64% active, and 36 ÷ 64 × 100 ≈ 56 dependants per hundred workers. A wide base loads the ratio with children, straining schools and clinics; a heavy top loads it with pensioners, straining pensions and hospitals.

questions.question: Describe the three classic pyramid shapes with example countries, and interpret South Africa's own pyramid, including the demographic dividend.
questions.expected_answer: The expansive pyramid is a true triangle: very broad base tapering rapidly to a narrow peak, each cohort smaller than the one below — high birth rates with high or recently high death rates, many children, few elderly, rapid growth and short life expectancy, as in Mali, Uganda and Angola. Its future is preloaded through population momentum: today's giant child cohorts become tomorrow's giant parent cohorts, so growth continues for decades even after fertility falls. The stationary pyramid has almost vertical sides, cohorts of nearly equal length narrowing only near the top: births balance deaths, growth is near zero and life expectancy long, approximated by Australia and Denmark. The constrictive pyramid is pinched at the base — fewer young children than young adults because fertility has dropped below replacement — swollen in the middle and substantial at the top; the population is ageing and headed for contraction, as in Japan, Italy and South Korea, where each decade leaves fewer workers under more pensioners. South Africa's pyramid is transitional, between expansive and stationary: a still fairly broad base (fertility about 2,3, just above replacement) that has stopped widening, a pronounced bulge through the twenties and thirties, sides tapering faster than a wealthy country's — carrying the scar of the Aids years in the middle-aged cohorts — and female-leaning top bars. The country currently holds an unusually large working-age share relative to dependants, a window called the demographic dividend, which converts into prosperity only if the economy can employ the bulge that creates it.
